title: Which approach fits my assessment?
intro: Six questions. No answers leave this page — nothing is stored or sent anywhere. You will get two to three recommended approaches with the reasoning.

questions.legend: 1. What is this assessment mainly for?
questions.hint: Pick the primary purpose; the other one can be secondary.

options.label: Helping students learn (practice, feedback while they still can improve)
Certifying what each student achieved (a grade that stands on its own)

questions.legend: 2. What must the grade be evidence of?
questions.hint: Think about what a passing grade claims the student can do.

options.label: A final product (essay, report, problem set)
The process and decisions behind the work (how they got there)
A live skill — thinking, solving or defending in real time
Working well with AI tools (using, checking, critiquing them)

questions.hint: What your timetable and rooms realistically allow.

options.label: Take-home only — no reliable class time
Some class time exists, plus take-home

questions.legend: 5. Is skillful AI use itself part of what students should learn?
questions.hint: Not whether AI is allowed — whether using it well is a course outcome.

options.label: Partly — worth practising, not worth grading on its own
No — it is at best a tool, never the target

questions.legend: 6. What grading support do you have?
questions.hint: TAs, tutors or a grading team you can rely on.

options.label: A grading team I can brief and calibrate
Very little — grading time is very tight

inclass-writing.name: In-class writing
inclass-writing.desc: Move writing into class time: short, unaided, low-stakes pieces.

links.label: Case A uses staged submissions + a defence instead

oral-checks.name: Oral checks (viva-lite)
oral-checks.desc: Short structured Q&A where students defend choices from their own work.

staged-submissions.name: Staged submissions
staged-submissions.desc: Build the artefact in graded stages; grade the checkpoints cheaply.

process-portfolio.name: Process portfolio
process-portfolio.desc: Grade drafts, logs and version history alongside the artefact.

local-data.name: Personalized or local data
local-data.desc: Run the task on data students collected or that belongs to this class.

critique-ai.name: Critiquing AI output
critique-ai.desc: Give students AI-produced work to find, fix and justify the errors.

open-ai-reflection.name: Open AI use with reflection
open-ai-reflection.desc: Allow full AI use; grade the log, the judgment and the reflection.

secure-checks.name: Proctored/secure checks
secure-checks.desc: Short supervised checks carrying the assurance weight; everything else stays open.

rules.why: Practice-focused assessment where AI skill is a goal is exactly the open-lane case: let AI in, grade the judgment.
Even without an explicit AI outcome, practice work loses little to open AI use when the log is graded instead of the answers.
You cannot teach AI judgment while banning AI; the reflection log makes the skill assessable.
Assurance claims need at least one condition the student does not fully control; regular class time makes short checks cheap.
At scale, short in-class checks beat individual orals on cost while carrying real weight.
A small secure component backs the certificate claim without policing everything.
If the outcome is thinking or defending in real time, the evidence has to be real-time — a short structured oral is the direct measure.
With a manageable cohort, orals on the student's own process are the strongest single authorship check.
With a team you can brief, sampled orals stay affordable (see the faculty notes on sampling).
Stages produce traceable process evidence without needing class time.
Even product-focused assurance improves when the artefact is built in checkpoints you can verify along the way.
When the journey is the evidence, logs and drafts need to be part of the grade.
Logs and reflections grade fast with a checklist rubric.
Generic AI output cannot match data your students collected; local data rebuilds the validity of a product task.
Collectable data also improves engagement — but its main job here is validity.
Critiquing AI work both teaches and measures the evaluation skill directly.
Find-and-fix items add evaluation practice with low grading cost.
One AI artefact serves a whole cohort, so critique items are among the cheapest to mark.
With a small cohort and weekly class time, in-class writing gives a strong product-to-student link — watch the equity notes (typing speed, accommodations).
In-class writing requires the class time you said you do not have.
At large scale, timed in-class writing amplifies accommodation logistics; short secure checks are cheaper.

alwaysAdd.note: Considered regardless of answers: an explicit AI-use level per stage (see the AIAS levels page) is worth adopting whatever else you choose.
